title: A secure signup route
idea: A signup route creates an account. It hashes the password, stores only the hash, and replies with the new user's id and email.
points: `bcrypt.hash(password, 10)` makes a one-way hash with a random salt mixed in.
`onConflictDoNothing()` lets the `unique` rule on `email` decide, even for simultaneous requests.
`returning` picks the columns to send back, so the hash never leaves.

messages.label: POST /auth/signup
messages.note: The client sends an email and a password as JSON.

messages.label: hash(password, 10)
messages.note: The handler hashes the password first. The plain text goes no further.

messages.label: salted hash
messages.note: bcrypt returns the hash. The same password gives a different hash each time.

messages.label: INSERT email, hash
messages.note: The handler inserts the email and the hash. The `unique` rule on `email` guards duplicates.

messages.label: id, email
messages.note: Postgres returns only the columns `returning` asked for. The hash is not among them.

messages.label: 201 { user }
messages.note: The client gets the new id and email. The hash never leaves the server.

messages.label: INSERT same email
messages.note: Now the same email signs up again. The `unique` rule refuses the row.

messages.label: no row
messages.note: `onConflictDoNothing()` turns the refusal into an empty result, not an exception.

messages.label: 409 Conflict
messages.note: No row came back, so the handler answers 409 with a clear message.

code.title: Signup controller
code.caption: The controller comes first. Everything after it is setup, so this file runs alone.

walk.text: Read the credentials from the JSON body. `express.json()` on line 32 fills it.
Hash the password. The salt is random and stored inside the hash. Cost 10 slows each guess.
Insert the email and the hash. The plain password is never stored.
On a duplicate email, do nothing instead of throwing.
Send back only `id` and `email`. `passwordHash` is not listed.
No row back means 409. Otherwise reply 201 with the new user.
Sign up twice, then check Postgres kept a hash, not the password.

pitfalls: Never store or log the plain password. Store the hash only.
Do not return the whole row. Choose columns in `returning`, or `passwordHash` leaks.
This route trusts the body. A missing or non-string password throws; the next lecture adds Zod.

quiz.q: The snippet posts the same signup twice. Which statuses print?
quiz.why: The first insert succeeds (201). The second breaks the `unique` rule on `email`, returns no row, and the handler sends 409.

takeaway: Hash the password, store only the hash, return only safe fields.

starters: Why bcrypt and not a fast hash like SHA-256?
What does the 10 in bcrypt.hash mean?
Why 409 and not 400 for a duplicate email?
